title: Robert Lefkowitz uncovered the receptors through which many drugs act, and won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry

trailer.text: Robert Lefkowitz is an American physician who in 1972 was recruited by Duke University Medical Center to develop a program in molecular cardiology there.
Robert Lefkowitz, born in New York in 1943 and holder of an M.D. from Columbia University, won the 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry together with Brian Kobilka.
Lefkowitz wrote that he is Jewish.
For a long time it remained a mystery how cells sense their environment, and in 1968 Lefkowitz began tracing cells' receptors using radioactivity.

In the 1980s his group, with the young physician Brian Kobilka, searched for the gene of the beta receptor, and the researchers realized that there is a whole family of receptors that are similar in structure and function in the same way.
According to the Swedish Academy, about half of all medications act through these receptors.

stations.title: A mystery in the cell wall

paragraphs.text: For a long time it remained a mystery how cells are able to sense their environment.
What the receptors consist of and how they work remained obscured for most of the 20th century.
In the 1940s the American scientist Raymond Ahlquist examined how different organs react to adrenalin-like substances.
At the end of the 19th century, scientists who suspected that adrenalin worked via nerves paralyzed the nervous system of laboratory animals, but the effect of the adrenalin remained.
The receptors were hard to trace because they are relatively few and mostly embedded in the cell wall.
According to Duke, senior scientists at that time doubted the very existence of receptors on the cell surface.

stations.title: A boy from Parkchester who wanted to be a doctor

paragraphs.text: Lefkowitz was born in 1943 and grew up in the Bronx, in an apartment complex called Parkchester.
Lefkowitz wrote that he is Jewish and that he attended a public high school in New York City.
As early as the third or fourth grade he decided that his family doctor was his occupational role model.
He said that he is the eighth Nobel laureate to have graduated from the Bronx High School of Science.
In 1962, at the age of 19, he graduated from Columbia and moved on to the university's medical school.
In 1966 he received an M.D. from Columbia University.
He completed his studies at the height of the Vietnam War and joined the U.S. Public Health Service to avoid service in Vietnam.
He was assigned for two years to the National Institutes of Health.

stations.title: 1968–1974: Radioactive iodine, despair and a breakthrough

paragraphs.text: In 1968 Lefkowitz began using radioactivity to trace cells' receptors.
He attached an iodine isotope to various hormones, and thanks to the radiation he unveiled several receptors.
Lefkowitz said that in his first year in the laboratory he failed at virtually everything he tried.
A year passed without progress, and he, who did not really want to do research, began to despair.
According to him, his father's death and the failures in the laboratory made 1968–69 one of the most difficult years of his life.
In the summer of 1969 his experiments began to bear fruit.
In 1970 he published articles in two leading journals, PNAS and Science.
In early 1971 he began the effort to prove the existence of beta-adrenergic receptors.
In the summer of 1972, Duke University Medical Center recruited him to develop a program in molecular cardiology.

According to Britannica, in 1972, while working in Boston in the laboratory of Edgar Haber, Lefkowitz published a report on the purification of the beta-adrenergic receptor protein from heart muscle cells of dogs.
In the spring of 1974, together with Marc Caron, he developed a radioactive binding assay for the beta-adrenergic receptor.

According to him, this development, alongside which similar approaches were also developed by Gerald Aurbach at the NIH and Alex Levitzki at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, finally opened the door to direct study of the receptors.

stations.title: The 1980s: The gene and the seven spirals

paragraphs.text: According to Duke, in the early 1980s the laboratory introduced a receptor protein into cells that did not respond to adrenaline, and the cells began to respond.
In the 1980s Lefkowitz decided that his group would try to find the gene that codes for the beta receptor.
In those years, finding a particular gene in the enormous genome was difficult and slow.
Lefkowitz recruited the young physician Brian Kobilka.
According to Lefkowitz, Kobilka joined his laboratory as a cardiology fellow in 1984.
Kobilka took on the challenge of isolating the gene of the beta-adrenergic receptor from the enormous human genome.
According to Snyderman, Kobilka's decision to clone the receptor through a genomic approach was bold, and some thought it harebrained.
According to Duke, in the mid-1980s the laboratory cloned the gene for the adrenaline receptor, and thus a new field of drug research opened.
Analysis of the gene showed that the receptor consists of seven spirals, meaning that it probably crosses the cell wall seven times.
Lefkowitz later described the discovery as a “real eureka moment”.
In his group, all four of the then known adrenergic receptor subtypes were isolated and their genes were cloned, and in this way a similarity to rhodopsin was discovered.
The researchers realized that there is a whole family of receptors that are similar in structure and function in the same way.
The mapping of the human genome revealed close to a thousand genes that code for G-protein–coupled receptors.
A single receptor can recognize several different hormones outside the cell.

stations.title: Seeing the receptor in action, and discovering beta-arrestin

paragraphs.text: After the gene was isolated, Kobilka moved to Stanford, and there he tried to create an image of the receptor, a goal that most of the scientific community considered unattainable.
G-protein–coupled receptors are by nature very mobile, but inside a crystal they must remain almost completely still, so crystallizing them is a challenge.
It took Kobilka more than two decades to find a solution to the imaging problems.
In 2011 he and his team captured an image of the beta-adrenergic receptor at the moment a hormone activates it.
According to Snyderman, these receptors signal through two pathways: via G proteins and via beta-arrestin.
According to Duke, beta-arrestin binds to the receptor and dampens its sensitivity or turns it off temporarily.
According to Snyderman, in 2004 Lefkowitz conceived the idea of the "biased" ligand, and by the next day he had secured 12 ligands to the angiotensin receptor.
Lefkowitz and his colleagues found ligands that stimulate signaling via beta-arrestin while at the same time blocking G protein responses.
He co-founded the company Trevena with Howard Rockman of Duke.

stations.title: The drugs that rely on the receptors

paragraphs.text: According to the Academy, about half of medications act through these receptors, among them beta blockers, antihistamines and psychiatric medications.
According to Duke, the receptors are the target of prescription drugs such as antihistamines, ulcer drugs and beta blockers.
Knowledge of the structure of the activated receptor is expected to be useful in the future for the development of new drugs.

stations.title: Nobel, awards and two hundred students

paragraphs.text: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences decided to award the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for 2012, and Lefkowitz won it together with Kobilka.
The prize amount, SEK 8 million, was to be shared equally between the two laureates.
The prize was scheduled to be presented at a ceremony in Stockholm on December 10.
Lefkowitz listed among his awards the National Medal of Science, the Shaw Prize, the Research Achievement Award of the American Heart Association and the BBVA Award.
According to Snyderman, he has won more than 60 important awards.
According to Lefkowitz, he became a Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator in 1976.
According to Duke, he is one of the longest-serving investigators in the history of the institute.
According to Duke, Lefkowitz spent 39 years of a research career at the Duke University Medical Center.
Lefkowitz has mentored more than 200 trainees.
The dean of Duke's School of Medicine said that he has had a profound influence on the careers of more than 200 students and postdoctoral fellows.
In 2021 Lefkowitz published a memoir.
He has five children.
According to the National Science Foundation (NSF), the National Medal of Science was presented to Lefkowitz by President George Bush in the East Room of the White House on September 29, 2008.
Lefkowitz, in his autobiography: in 2010
Some disputed that the prize for this work belongs to chemistry.
A blogger at Scientific American replied that the binding of a small molecule to a receptor is a molecular interaction as much as anything in chemistry.

In 2021 Lefkowitz published a memoir titled A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to Stockholm: The Adrenaline-Fueled Adventures of an Accidental Scientist.

claims.text: סכום הפרס הוא 8 מיליון כתר שוודי, שיחולק שווה בשווה בין שני הזוכים.
claims.quote: The Prize amount: SEK 8 million, to be shared equally between the Laureates.

claims.text: הזוכים יקבלו את הפרס בטקס בסטוקהולם ב-10 בדצמבר.
claims.quote: They will receive the Nobel Prize in Stockholm at a Dec. 10 ceremony.

claims.text: לפקוביץ מנה בין פרסיו את מדליית המדע הלאומית ופרס שו, שניהם ב-2007.
claims.quote: The National Medal of Science (2007); The Shaw Prize in Life Science and Medicine (2007)

claims.text: לפקוביץ מנה את פרס ההישג המחקרי של איגוד הלב האמריקאי (2009) ופרס BBVA (2010).
claims.quote: Research Achievement Award, American Heart Association (2009); BBVA Foundation Frontiers of Knowledge Award (2010)

claims.text: לפי סניידרמן, לפקוביץ זכה ביותר מ-60 פרסים חשובים.
claims.quote: Bob has been widely recognized with more than 60 important awards, of which 10 are represented here

claims.text: לפי לפקוביץ, הוא הפך לחוקר של מכון הווארד יוז ב-1976.
claims.quote: I became an HHMI Investigator 37 years ago in 1976

claims.text: לפי דיוק, הוא אחד החוקרים הוותיקים בהיסטוריה של מכון הווארד יוז (36 שנים).
claims.quote: one of the longest-serving Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigators in history (36 years)

claims.text: לפי דיוק, לפקוביץ העביר את כל 39 שנות הקריירה המחקרית שלו במרכז הרפואי של דיוק.
claims.quote: has spent his entire 39-year research career at the Duke University Medical Center

claims.text: דיקן בית הספר לרפואה של דיוק אמרה שלפקוביץ השפיע השפעה עמוקה על הקריירות של יותר מ-200 סטודנטים ועמיתי פוסט-דוקטורט.
claims.quote: he has had a profound influence on the careers of more than 200 students and postdoctoral fellows.

claims.text: לפי סניידרמן, לפקוביץ מנה חמישה ילדים וארבעה נכדים ואת אשתו לין.
claims.quote: 5 children, 4 grandchildren, and his wife Lynn

claims.text: הבלוגר טען שקשירת מולקולה קטנה לקולטן היא אינטראקציה מולקולרית כמו כל דבר בכימיה, בתגובה לעוררין על כך שהפרס שייך לכימיה.
claims.quote: Binding of a small molecule to a GPCR is as much of a molecular interaction as anything in chemistry.

claims.text: לפי דיוק, קובילקה היה עמית פוסט-דוקטורט בקרדיולוגיה בדיוק בין 1984 ל-1989.
claims.quote: Kobilka was a post-doctoral fellow in cardiology at Duke from 1984 to 1989 and part of Lefkowitz's lab.

claims.text: לפי דיוק, קובילקה הצטרף לסגל סטנפורד ב-1990.
claims.quote: He joined the faculty of medicine and molecular and cellular physiology at Stanford in 1990.

claims.text: לפי בלוג של סיינטיפיק אמריקן, כ-30% מכלל התרופות מכוונות לקולטנים מצומדי חלבון G.
claims.quote: GPCRs are also immensely important in medicine and are the target of about 30% of all drugs.

claims.text: לפקוביץ סיפר שבזמן כתיבת האוטוביוגרפיה היו לו חמישה נכדים.
claims.quote: At the time of this writing I have five grandchildren

claims.text: לפי לפקוביץ, הוא בילה 40 שנות קריירה בדיוק; הוא מתאר "40 year career at Duke".
claims.quote: For the first 20 of my 40 year career at Duke, I focused on three essential questions about G protein coupled receptors

claims.text: לפי הבלוגר, ב-12 השנים האחרונות פוענחו יותר מttuzin מבנים גבישיים של קולטנים מצומדי חלבון G.
claims.quote: In the last 12 years more than a dozen GPCR crystal structures have been resolved.

claims.text: לפי הקרן הלאומית למדע (NSF), מדליית המדע הלאומית הוענקה ללפקוביץ מידי הנשיא ג'ורג' בוש באולם המזרחי של הבית הלבן ב-29 בספטמבר 2008.
claims.quote: Presented by President George W. Bush in the East Room of the White House on September 29, 2008.

claims.text: רוברט לפקוביץ, יליד ניו יורק ב-1943 ובעל תואר דוקטור לרפואה מאוניברסיטת קולומביה, זכה ב-2012 בפרס נובל בכימיה יחד עם בריאן קובילקה.
claims.quote: Robert Joseph Lefkowitz, 1943–, American physician, b. New York, N.Y., M.D. Columbia, 1966.

claims.text: רוברט לפקוביץ, יליד ניו יורק ב-1943 ובעל תואר דוקטור לרפואה מאוניברסיטת קולומביה, זכה ב-2012 בפרס נובל בכימיה יחד עם בריאן קובילקה.
